title: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 90)
hookLine: a thousand years are like yesterday; teach us to count our days
last: EVEN THE SPARROW HAS A HOME.

cards: Some people keep a jar of marbles on a shelf: one for every Saturday they might reasonably have left, worked out from their age. Every Saturday morning, they take one out and drop it in a bowl. It sounds grim.
Some who try it say the opposite: the shrinking jar makes the Saturdays better. They stop wasting them. That idea is very old.
A psalm whose heading carries the name of Moses is about exactly this: the shortness of a life held against the length of God, and a request to learn how to count.

teach.b: The heading reads, "A Prayer of Moses the man of God." It starts with God's size: "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations." Before the mountains were born, you were God.
Then it zooms out until time itself shrinks: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night." A watch was a few hours of guard duty.
A thousand years, gone like a night shift. Next to that, human life looks like grass, the psalm says, green in the morning and cut down by evening.
It even gives a number: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten." Seventy. Eighty, if strong.
"For it is soon cut off, and we fly away." This could have ended in gloom. Instead it turns into a request.
"So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

teach.h: TEACH US TO COUNT, NOT TO FEAR
teach.b: To number is to count, the way you'd count coins. The same root shows up in the writing on the wall in the book of Daniel: mene, numbered. The psalm doesn't ask to be spared the counting.
It asks to be taught to count well, so the counting turns into wisdom instead of fear.

teach.h: ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS
teach.b: And the last verse asks for something lasting: "establish thou the work of our hands."

teach.h: SO TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.
teach.b: Isaac Watts turned this psalm into a hymn, now usually sung as O God, Our Help in Ages Past, and it's still sung at funerals and remembrance services.

how: Psalm 90 is often read at Christian funerals and on New Year's Eve, and Isaac Watts's hymn based on it, "O God, Our Help in Ages Past," is sung at memorials and remembrance services.

games.q: you've just admitted that life is short: grass in the morning, gone by evening. what do you ask for?
o: to be taught to count my days, and grow wise.
games.why: "so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." the psalm turns the counting into a lesson, not a fear.

practice: Count the days left in this month, on your fingers if you like, and hold the number. Then let a few of those days come to mind one at a time, not as a to-do list, and ask of each: what would make this day worth keeping?
If you pray, say the psalm's line, so teach us to number our days; if you don't, just hold the number gently, without panic.

wordCard.voice: Mene. The word numbered from the writing on the wall in Daniel, sharing its root with this psalm's prayer to count our days well.

orig.note: Hebrew: to count, to number. the same root gives mene, numbered, in the writing on the wall in Daniel.

carryVoice: Your line: number our days. Counted well, they turn into wisdom, not fear. See you tomorrow.
